newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan commodity trade unchanged by govt sacking.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan commodity trade unchanged by govt sacking.

text.p: Pakistani officials and traders said on Thursday they did not expect major changes in trade flows after the dismissal of former prime minister Benazir Bhutto's government.

"We have not received any new instructions to hold back or cancel any deals and I do not think the trade policy is going to go through a major change just because a new set of rulers have taken charge in Islamabad," an official of the state-run Trading Corporation (TCP) of Pakistan said.
Pakistan's main trading house, TCP deals mainly in the imports of vegetable oils and sugar and the export of rice for state-run organisations.
Officials said TCP had imported a total of 236,000 tonnes of sugar in 1996 while private importers had bought in more than 150,000 tonnes.
Saulat Enterprises, a private trading house, said Pakistan imported a total of 97,244 tonnes of vegoil in October, up from 92,062 tonnes imported in September.
Traders said Pakistan's vegoil imports will also pick up ahead of the holy month of Ramadan, which starts in mid-January.
"Presently it is the cottonseed oil season and it is in good supply in the market," one trader said.
"But keeping in view the rise in demand during Ramadan, most traders will start building up their positions in December," he said.
The trader said domestic vegoil supplies usually keep a lid on imports between September and February, but Ramadan, which changes dates each year, falls during that period in 1997.
On sugar imports, the trader said the crushing season that starts this month will keep down imports until next April or May, when TCP and private importers will have a better idea of domestic needs.
The private Pakistan Sugar Mills Association said some 250,000 to 300,000 tonnes of sugar may be imported between May and November 1997.
Pakistan produced 2.47 million tonnes of sugar in 1995/96 (July-June), 130,000 million tonnes short of total estimated domestic demand of 2.6 million.

An official at the state-run Rice Export Corporation, whose chairman Syed Muhammad Ishaq was relieved of his duty this morning as part of a shakeup in the bureaucratic struture by the new government, said "nothing will change."
"Officials come and go but functioning of institutions will continue smoothly," he said.
